title: A frenzy of stars
caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy IC 4710, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IC 4710 · constellation Pavo · about 25 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A busy cloud of bright stars fills this Hubble image, with bright pockets scattered around its edges where bursts of new stars are forming. This is IC 4710, a dwarf irregular galaxy discovered in 1900 by astronomer DeLisle Stewart.

Irregular galaxies live up to their name. They look chaotic, with no central bulge and no spiral arms, setting them apart from spirals and ellipticals. Astronomers think some may once have been spirals or ellipticals that were pulled out of shape over time by the gravity of other galaxies during encounters or mergers.

Dwarf irregulars matter especially for understanding how galaxies change over cosmic time, because they are thought to resemble the very first galaxies that formed in the Universe. Studying nearby examples like IC 4710 gives a closer look at objects that may be similar to those early systems.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.29 x 2.99 arcminutes) and distance (25 million light years), the frame spans roughly 24,000 × 22,000 light-years. Its light set out about 25 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

explore: The galaxy sits in Pavo, the Peacock, a southern constellation, roughly 25 million light-years from us. Pavo is also home to NGC 6752, ranked the third-brightest globular cluster in our sky, NGC 6744, a spiral galaxy, as well as six known planetary systems, including HD 181433, which hosts a super-Earth.
alt: A loose, busy cloud of bright stars with brighter pockets scattered around its edges.
